subject: organic-chemistry
title: Bonding and hybridization
summary: How carbon forms bonds, the shapes that result, and how to draw Lewis structures with formal charges and resonance.

concepts.name: Orbital hybridization
concepts.summary: Carbon's s and p orbitals mix into hybrid orbitals whose number and shape match the atom's electron domains.

explain.text: Carbon's 2s and 2p orbitals can mix into new orbitals called hybrid orbitals, which point in the directions the bonds actually take. The number of hybrid orbitals always equals the number of atomic orbitals that were mixed. One s and three p orbitals make four sp³ orbitals, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, as in methane, CH₄. One s and two p orbitals make three sp² orbitals in a flat triangle, with one p orbital left over, as in ethene. One s and one p orbital make two sp orbitals in a straight line, as in ethyne. Hybridization explains bond angles that unmixed orbitals cannot.

concepts.name: Sigma and pi bonds
concepts.summary: A sigma bond overlaps head-on along the bond axis, a pi bond overlaps side by side, and a multiple bond has one sigma bond plus pi bonds.

explain.text: A covalent bond is made by overlapping orbitals. A sigma bond forms when orbitals overlap head-on along the line joining two nuclei. Every single bond is a sigma bond. A pi bond forms when parallel p orbitals overlap side by side, above and below that line. A double bond has one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds. Pi bonds are weaker and do not let the atoms turn freely, which is why alkenes stay flat around their double bond. Counting sigma and pi bonds is a quick check on any structure.

concepts.name: Formal charge
concepts.summary: The charge an atom would have if its bonding electrons were shared equally, used to check and compare Lewis structures.

elements.name: Formal charges on oxygen and nitrogen
Choosing Lewis structures by formal charge

explain.text: Formal charge is the charge an atom would have if every bonding electron were shared equally between the atoms it is bonded to. It is found with valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus the number of bonds. Each bond gives one of its electrons to each atom it joins. For example, in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, nitrogen has five valence electrons, no nonbonding electrons and four bonds, so its formal charge is 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Formal charges help choose the best Lewis structure: smaller charges are better, and a negative charge belongs on the more electronegative atom.

concepts.name: Resonance structures
concepts.summary: Two or more Lewis structures that differ only in electron placement, which together describe one delocalized molecule.

explain.text: Some molecules cannot be drawn with one Lewis structure. Resonance structures are two or more Lewis structures that differ only in where the pi bonds and lone pairs sit, not in how the atoms are joined. The real molecule is a resonance hybrid, an average of them. Electrons move with curved arrows, from a lone pair or pi bond toward an atom or bond, and atoms never move. Ozone, O₃, is the classic example: two equivalent forms put the double bond on different oxygens, which makes both oxygen–oxygen bonds the same length. Forms with full octets and small formal charges contribute most.

concepts.name: Bond dipoles
concepts.summary: Unequal sharing in a bond gives it a dipole, and a molecule's net dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles.

explain.text: A bond dipole is the separation of charge in a bond between atoms of different electronegativity. The bonding electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative atom, which becomes partly negative, while the other atom becomes partly positive. Chemists draw a dipole as an arrow pointing toward the negative end, with a plus sign at its tail. Bond dipoles are vectors, so a molecule's overall dipole depends on their directions as well as their sizes. In carbon dioxide the two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. In water the two O–H dipoles add to a net dipole.

items.prompt: What hybridization does the carbon atom in methane, CH₄, have?
items.explanation: Carbon in CH₄ has four bonding regions and no lone pairs, so it makes four hybrid orbitals, all sp³. sp³d would need five regions, and sp and sp² give only two and three.

items.prompt: How many hybrid orbitals form when one s orbital and two p orbitals are mixed?
items.explanation: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: one s plus two p gives three, which is sp². Four would be sp³, which mixes three p orbitals.

items.prompt: Which shape do the four sp³ hybrid orbitals of carbon point toward?
items.explanation: Four orbitals spread as far apart as possible point to the corners of a tetrahedron, about 109.5° apart. A straight line is sp, a flat triangle is sp², and a square plane is not an sp³ shape.

items.prompt: Which hybridization does each carbon in ethyne, HC≡CH, have?
items.explanation: Each carbon bonds to two atoms and has no lone pair, so it has two electron domains and is sp. A triple bond still counts as one region for hybridization, which is why sp² is a tempting but wrong answer.

items.prompt: What is the hybridization of each carbon in ethene, H₂C=CH₂?
items.explanation: Each carbon has three electron domains: two C–H bonds and the C=C double bond, which counts as one region. That gives sp². sp³ is the mistake of counting the double bond as two regions.

items.prompt: The oxygen in H₂O has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. How many electron domains does it have, and what hybridization follows?
items.explanation: Two bonds plus two lone pairs give four domains, so the oxygen is sp³. A lone pair takes a hybrid orbital just as a bond does. Counting only the bonds gives two, the mistake behind sp.

items.prompt: The boron in BF₃ has three bonding regions and no lone pairs. Which hybridization does it have?
items.explanation: Three regions give three hybrid orbitals, sp², in a flat triangle. sp³ would need four regions, which BF₃ does not have.

items.prompt: The carbon in the methyl anion, CH₃⁻, has three bonds and one lone pair. What is its hybridization?
items.explanation: Four electron domains, counting the lone pair, give four hybrid orbitals: sp³. The common mistake is to count only the three bonds and answer sp².

items.prompt: Put these steps for finding the hybridization of a central atom in order.
steps: Draw the Lewis structure of the molecule
Count the electron domains around the central atom
Match the count to the hybridization: two is sp, three is sp², four is sp³
items.explanation: The count comes from the Lewis structure, and the match needs the count, so the steps must run in this order.

items.prompt: How many sigma bonds does a carbon–carbon double bond contain?
items.explanation: A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond. Two is tempting only if you count the double bond as two bonds of the same kind.

items.prompt: Which overlap forms a pi bond?
choices: Head-on overlap of two sp³ hybrid orbitals
Side-by-side overlap of two parallel p orbitals
items.explanation: A pi bond forms when parallel p orbitals overlap side by side, above and below the bond axis. Head-on overlaps, of hybrids or s orbitals, form sigma bonds.

items.prompt: How many pi bonds does a molecule of nitrogen, N≡N, contain?
items.explanation: A triple bond is one sigma bond plus two pi bonds. Three is the total number of bonds, not the number of pi bonds.

items.prompt: Ethyne, H–C≡C–H, contains how many sigma bonds and how many pi bonds?
items.explanation: Ethyne has three sigma bonds (two C–H and one C–C) and two pi bonds from its triple bond. Five is the number of shared electron pairs, not the number of sigma bonds.

items.prompt: How many pi bonds does ethene, H₂C=CH₂, have?
items.explanation: The C=C double bond contributes one pi bond, and every C–H bond is sigma. Two would be right only if the double bond were a triple bond.

items.prompt: Why is rotation about a C=C double bond restricted?
choices: The pi bond's side-by-side overlap would break if the carbons turned
The sigma bond must break before the carbons can turn
The double bond has no electron density, so it cannot turn
items.explanation: Turning the carbons would misalign the p orbitals and break the pi bond, which costs a lot of energy. The sigma bond is symmetrical around its axis and can turn; the double bond does have electron density.

items.prompt: Which hybrid orbitals does each carbon in ethyne use for its sigma bonds?
items.explanation: Each carbon is sp, so two hybrid orbitals make its sigma bonds. The two unhybridized p orbitals on each carbon make the two pi bonds. Ethyne is linear, so sp³ is wrong.

items.prompt: In formaldehyde, H₂C=O, how many sigma and pi bonds does the carbon form in total?
items.explanation: The carbon has two C–H single bonds and a C=O double bond, which adds one sigma and one pi. That totals three sigma and one pi. Counting the double bond's pi as two gives 3 sigma, 2 pi.

items.prompt: Put these steps for building a C=C double bond in order.
steps: Two sp² orbitals overlap head-on to make a sigma bond between the carbons
Once the sigma bond holds the carbons in place, the unhybridized p orbital on each carbon is parallel to the other
The parallel p orbitals overlap side by side, above and below the bond axis, to make a pi bond
items.explanation: The sigma bond forms first and fixes the positions of the carbons. Only then are the p orbitals parallel to each other, and their side-by-side overlap makes the pi bond.

items.prompt: Which expression gives the formal charge of an atom in a Lewis structure?
items.explanation: Formal charge is valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus the number of bonds. Adding nonbonding electrons, or adding the bonds, gives the wrong result.

items.prompt: What is the formal charge on the oxygen in water, H₂O?
items.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons, four nonbonding (two lone pairs) and two bonds: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0.

items.prompt: What is the formal charge on the oxygen in hydronium, H₃O⁺?
items.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons, two nonbonding (one lone pair) and three bonds: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. The ion's overall +1 charge sits on oxygen.

items.prompt: What is the formal charge on the oxygen in hydroxide, OH⁻?
items.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons, six nonbonding (three lone pairs) and one bond: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. A charge of −2 would need the oxygen to have two bonds.

items.prompt: In the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, drawn with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds, what is the formal charge on the nitrogen?
items.explanation: Nitrogen has five valence electrons, no nonbonding electrons and four bonds, since the double bond counts twice: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

items.prompt: In the same nitrate ion, what is the formal charge on an oxygen that is single-bonded to the nitrogen and has three lone pairs?
items.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons, six nonbonding and one bond: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. This single-bonded oxygen carries the ion's negative charge.

items.prompt: Which rule is used to choose between Lewis structures by their formal charges?
choices: Larger formal charges are better, and negative charge goes on the less electronegative atom
Only atoms bonded to hydrogen can carry formal charges
Smaller formal charges are better, and negative charge goes on the more electronegative atom
items.explanation: Structures whose formal charges are closer to zero are preferred, and a negative charge belongs on the more electronegative atom. The first choice reverses both rules.

items.prompt: The carbon in the methyl anion, CH₃⁻, has three bonds and one lone pair. What is its formal charge?
items.explanation: Carbon has four valence electrons, two nonbonding (one lone pair) and three bonds: 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. Counting the lone pair as zero electrons would give +1, which is wrong.

items.prompt: Put these steps for finding formal charges on a Lewis structure in order.
steps: Draw the Lewis structure with all valence electrons placed
For each atom, count its nonbonding electrons and its bonds
Subtract those counts from the atom's valence electrons
items.explanation: The nonbonding electrons can only be counted once the Lewis structure exists, and the subtraction needs both counts.

items.prompt: What changes when one resonance structure is turned into another?
choices: Pi or lone-pair electrons move, while the atoms stay put
The number of valence electrons changes
A sigma bond breaks and reforms
items.explanation: Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are; the nuclei stay where they are. Breaking a sigma bond would change the molecule itself.

items.prompt: What is a resonance hybrid?
choices: One of the resonance structures drawn in a textbook
A molecule that rapidly flips between two shapes
The real molecule, an average of its resonance structures
A mixture of two different compounds
items.explanation: No single drawing is the real molecule. The resonance hybrid is the actual electron distribution, an average of the forms. A molecule that flips between two shapes describes a different idea.

items.prompt: How many equivalent resonance structures does ozone, O₃, have?
items.explanation: The double bond can sit on either terminal oxygen, giving two equivalent forms. One drawing alone cannot show that both oxygen–oxygen bonds are the same length.

items.prompt: Which statement about resonance structures is true?
choices: They are different compounds that can be separated
They have the same atom connections but different electron placements
items.explanation: Resonance structures keep every atom bonded the same way and move only electrons. Structures with different atom connections are isomers, which are different compounds.

items.prompt: How many equivalent resonance structures are usually drawn for the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻?
items.explanation: The double bond can sit on any of the three oxygens, giving three equivalent forms. Two would be right only if one of the oxygens were different from the others.

items.prompt: Which trait makes a resonance structure a major contributor to the hybrid?
choices: It has full octets and fewer formal charges
It puts a negative charge on the least electronegative atom
items.explanation: Structures with full octets and small formal charges contribute most. Putting a negative charge on the least electronegative atom is unfavorable, and more formal charges mean less stability.

items.prompt: Electrons in a resonance hybrid are called delocalized. What does that mean?
choices: They are fixed to one atom and cannot move
They are spread over several atoms instead of sitting on one
They have been removed from the molecule
items.explanation: Delocalized electrons are shared over more than two atoms, which stabilizes the molecule. Electrons fixed to one atom would be localized.

items.prompt: How many resonance forms are usually drawn for the allyl cation, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺?
items.explanation: The double bond and the positive charge can swap places across the three carbons, giving two forms, with the charge on each end carbon. The middle carbon never carries the charge.

items.prompt: Why are all six C–C bonds in benzene the same length?
choices: Each bond is an average of a single and a double bond, so they match
Each bond is a triple bond shortened by the ring
The bonds rotate so each one is briefly double
items.explanation: Benzene's resonance hybrid spreads its six pi electrons evenly over the ring, so every bond is between a single and a double bond in character. The bonds are not triple, and they do not rotate.

verification.note: b's note: Strictly, resonance hybrid delocalization, not literal averaging of two forms, but best choice.

items.prompt: Put these steps for drawing resonance forms in order.
steps: Draw one valid Lewis structure for the molecule
Move a pi bond or lone pair next to an atom with curved arrows to make a new form
Check that each new form has the same atoms and the right total valence electrons
Compare the forms and weight those with fewer formal charges more
items.explanation: The first form comes first, each new form is made by moving electrons and then checked, and only checked forms can be compared.

items.prompt: In a bond between two different atoms, which end is partly negative?
choices: Neither end, because the bond is covalent
items.explanation: The bonding electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative atom, which becomes partly negative. A bond between identical atoms has no dipole.

items.prompt: How is a bond dipole drawn as an arrow?
choices: Pointing toward the less electronegative atom, with a minus at its tail
Drawn as a double-headed arrow between the atoms
Pointing toward the more electronegative atom, with a plus at its tail
items.explanation: The arrow points toward the negative end, and a plus sign at its tail marks the positive end. Drawing the arrow the other way is a common error.

items.prompt: Which of these bonds is the most polar?
items.explanation: O–H has the largest electronegativity difference of these bonds, so its electrons are pulled most strongly toward oxygen. C–C and N–N bonds join identical atoms and are nonpolar.

items.prompt: The two C=O bond dipoles in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, point in which directions?
choices: At right angles, so they add to a larger dipole
items.explanation: The molecule is linear, and the two bond dipoles lie along one line in opposite directions, so the net dipole is zero. Carbon dioxide is nonpolar.

items.prompt: Why does water have a net dipole, rather than its two O–H dipoles cancelling?
choices: Because lone pairs cancel bond dipoles
Because the molecule is bent, so the two bond dipoles point partly the same way
items.explanation: Water's bent shape means the two O–H dipoles share a component in the same direction, so they add. A linear geometry would have cancelled them.

items.prompt: Which molecule has polar bonds but a net dipole of zero?
items.explanation: The four C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel. H₂O and NH₃ are bent or pyramidal, and HCl has a single bond dipole, so each has a net dipole.

items.prompt: How are bond dipoles combined to find a molecule's net dipole?
choices: Add their sizes only, ignoring direction
Add them as vectors, so direction matters
Keep only the largest one and ignore the rest
items.explanation: Bond dipoles have direction, so they must be added as vectors. Adding sizes alone gives the wrong answer for bent or symmetric molecules.

items.prompt: Two equal polar bonds, each with its dipole pointing from a central atom A toward a B atom, form a bent AB₂ molecule. Which statement is true?
choices: The net dipole is zero, since two equal dipoles always cancel
The net dipole points along the A–B bond line, away from both B atoms
The net dipole is nonzero and points along the bisector of the B–A–B angle, toward the two B atoms
items.explanation: Two equal dipoles cancel only when they point in opposite directions, as in a linear molecule. In a bent molecule their sum points along the bisector of the angle, toward the B atoms.

items.prompt: Put these steps for finding whether a molecule has a net dipole in order.
steps: Draw the molecule's shape from its Lewis structure
Mark each bond dipole, pointing toward the more electronegative atom
Add the bond dipoles as vectors
If the sum is zero, the molecule is nonpolar; otherwise it has a net dipole
items.explanation: The shape is needed to see the directions, the dipoles must be marked before they are added, and the sum decides the answer last.
